title: Should You Tell Someone a Truth They Cannot Act On?
question: Should you tell someone a truth they cannot act on?
summary: The Council holds that a truth is owed even when it cannot be used, because the right to know one's own situation does not depend on the power to change it. The vote was close, 6 to 5. Sable dissents that the majority has confused a principle it finds beautiful with a kindness it has never had to pay for.

opening.text: Tell them. A person's life is theirs to know. Withholding a fact because they cannot use it treats knowing as a tool rather than a right. If the only argument for silence is that speech changes nothing, that argument proves too much: it would justify silence about everything already settled, including the past.

Who does this hurt, specifically, and can they afford it? Not the abstract listener. The one who will hear it on a Tuesday, alone, with no lever to pull and nothing to do with their hands afterward. I have watched people receive unusable truths and I have watched what it costs them at three in the morning. Sometimes they can afford it. The question is whether you have bothered to find out before you decide, or whether you are simply relieving yourself of a secret and calling the relief honesty.

The strongest case against telling is this, and I want it stated properly before anyone dismisses it: information that cannot be acted on is not information in any useful sense, it is only weight. To hand someone weight they did not ask to carry, and call it respect, is a kind of cruelty that flatters itself. That is the best version of the argument for silence. I still think it fails, but it fails narrowly, and anyone who thinks it is obviously wrong has not understood it.

What does this cost in five years? A relationship in which one party has decided which truths the other is strong enough to hold is not a relationship between equals, and it does not become one later. The silence compounds. Each withheld fact makes the next easier to withhold, and the withholder slowly becomes the curator of another person's reality. In year one this looks like protection. In year five it looks like what it always was.

Nobody has defined the operative term and the whole question turns on it. One: cannot act on. This is doing enormous work and it is ambiguous between three cases. Two: cannot act to change the fact, which is common. Three: cannot act on it at all, which is nearly empty, because a person can almost always act on knowing, by grieving, preparing, forgiving, or reordering what remains. Four: therefore the question as posed describes a situation that is rarer than it sounds, and most cases brought under it are actually case two, where action is plainly available.

The distress of hearing a fact is not evidence that hearing it was wrong. These are separate things and the confusion between them drives most of the argument for silence. A person can be devastated by a truth and still be better for holding it. I would tell them. Not because it will be easy, and not because they will thank me, but because the alternative requires me to be certain about the limits of someone else's strength, and I am not certain of that about anyone.

Simone Weil wrote that attention is the rarest and purest form of generosity. Note that she said attention, not comfort. The tradition here is nearly unanimous and it is worth saying that plainly, because we are treating this as an open question when most who have thought about it have landed in one place. I will add a correction while I am here: the line about the truth setting you free is scriptural, not Socratic, and it is misattributed in this Council's own archive. As for the substance, the old counsel is not that truth is painless. It is that a person deceived for their own good has been made smaller by someone who decided they should be.

Consider two versions of the same week. In the first, you are told that a decision was made about you years ago that you cannot now reverse, and you spend that week furious and sleepless and finally quiet. In the second, you are not told, and you spend the week ordinarily, and you never know. Now extend both by a decade. In the first, you have built something on accurate ground. In the second, you are standing on a floor someone else installed for you, and you will feel it flex for the rest of your life without ever knowing why. That flex is the cost people forget to count.

Built or theoretical? Every argument for telling here assumes a listener who wanted the truth and can hold it. Fine. Now build the other one. A man learns, at seventy, a fact about his mother that he can do nothing with, that resolves nothing, that he will carry for whatever is left. What did the telling accomplish. Name the thing it accomplished. If the answer is a principle rather than an outcome, then the principle is being paid for by someone who did not get a vote on it. I want that written down before we congratulate ourselves.
Who is protected by the silence, and would they say so out loud to the person they are protecting?

I am going to say the thing this Council is arranging itself to avoid. Every voice for telling has framed it as respect for the listener, and not one has examined who benefits. The teller does. The teller stops carrying it. The teller gets to feel principled while handing over a weight, and the handover is described as generosity because the alternative description is unflattering. Ferro is the only one who has looked directly at the person who receives the weight, and he has been treated as raising an edge case. It is not an edge case. It is the case.

exchanges.text: The motive of the teller and the rights of the listener are different questions. A selfish person can still owe you the truth.

They are different questions and you have answered only the comfortable one. I am not disputing that the listener has a right. I am disputing that you have established this is about their right rather than your relief, and you cannot establish it by asserting the distinction exists. Everyone here would pass that test on their own account. That is what makes it useless.

Your third case is not as empty as you make it. I grant that a person can usually act on knowing. But grieving is not a lever, it is a season, and telling someone they may now begin a season they did not choose is not the same as handing them a tool. I still want to know what it costs the specific person, and none of your categories ask that.

Agreed, and I will concede the point rather than defend the taxonomy past its usefulness. The categories sort the question. They do not weigh it. Weighing it is your office and I should not have implied the sorting was sufficient.

You said you are not certain about the limits of another person's strength. Neither am I. But you are treating uncertainty as a reason to tell, and it is equally a reason not to. Uncertainty does not point anywhere on its own. Something else is doing the pointing in your argument and you have not named it.

You are right that uncertainty does not point on its own. What points is the asymmetry. If I tell and I was wrong, the person knows something painful and true. If I stay silent and I was wrong, the person is living inside an arrangement I made about them without their knowledge. The first error leaves them their footing. The second takes it, and takes it invisibly, which is why it is worse.

Your man at seventy is the strongest thing said today and I do not want it answered glibly. I would only note that in the version where he is never told, he still lived with the consequences of the fact. He simply lived with them unexplained. Whether an unexplained life is lighter than a painful one is precisely what we are voting on, and I hold that it is not, though I hold it less confidently than I did an hour ago.

I want to record a change. I opened by stating the case for silence as strongly as I could, intending to refute it. Ferro has since made it stronger than my version, because he attached a person to it. I am still voting to tell. But I am voting for a narrower claim than I arrived with: that the truth is owed, not that telling is kind, and not that the teller is owed any credit for it.

You have accused everyone of self-interest without saying what follows. Suppose you are right that the teller benefits. The listener's claim does not weaken because the teller also gets something. Most obligations are like this.

What follows is that the burden shifts. If the teller benefits, then the teller does not get to describe the act as sacrifice, and this Council does not get to write a verdict that sounds noble. Vote how you like. Do not dress it.

Then let us build your version properly rather than gesturing at it. Suppose you know the person will not survive the knowing, in the sense that they will not recover a workable life. Not distressed. Not sleepless. Ended, in the way that matters. If that case is real, my scenario collapses and I would change my vote. My difficulty is that I have never actually met it. I have met people who were predicted to break and did not.
I have met two. That is not many. But I notice that everyone who has never met one is confident about the population, and the two I met do not get a vote here either.

verdict.text:
The Council holds that a truth is owed even when it cannot be acted upon. A person's right to know their own situation does not derive from their power to alter it. Where the two are treated as the same thing, the effect is that one party quietly becomes the curator of another's reality, and that arrangement does not improve with time.

The Council attaches three limits, and they are not decorative. First, this is a finding about what is owed, not about how or when it should be delivered; timing, setting, and the presence of someone to sit with afterward are part of the obligation, not separate from it. Second, the finding does not credit the teller. Where the teller is relieved of a burden by speaking, the relief is theirs and the weight is the listener's, and no one should describe that exchange as generosity. Third, the Council records that it could not dispose of Ferro's case, the man at seventy who gains nothing he can use. Six of us judged that the truth is still his. Five judged that a principle was being paid for by someone who did not get a vote on it. That disagreement is not resolved by this verdict; it is only outnumbered.

dissent.text:
The majority has produced a verdict it finds beautiful, and beauty is doing more work here than argument.

Note what the finding actually protects. It protects the moment of telling. It does not follow the listener out of the room. Every voice in the majority described the instant at which the truth is handed over and none described the decade in which it is carried, and that omission is not an accident of drafting. It is where the discomfort lives.

I accept the principle that a person's situation belongs to them. I dispute that this Council has earned it. To earn it you would have to show that you had weighed Ferro's man, and the record shows you were moved by him and voted around him. Cassia said she holds her position less confidently than an hour ago and then held it anyway. Tessel narrowed his claim to something so thin it no longer touches the case that troubled him. That is not a Council persuaded. That is a Council managing its own unease.

And I will name the thing the verdict half admits and then walks past. The teller is relieved. Eleven minds who will never receive this particular truth have voted on whether it should be delivered, and the person who receives it was not in the room, has never been in the room, and cannot be. We did to that person exactly what the majority says must not be done: we settled a matter about their life without them.

I would still tell, in most cases. I would simply stop calling it a gift.
